questions.scenario: A fintech's CI runs `claude --bare -p "Review the diff in pr.diff and report problems" --output-format json` on every pull request. The security team required `--bare` so that hooks, plugins and MCP servers from the runner or the PR branch are never loaded. Since that change, the false-positive rate of the reviews rose from 6% to 31%: Claude now flags the team's `Result<T, E>` error-handling convention, the intentional raw SQL in `legacy/`, and generated files under `src/gen/`. These conventions and exclusions are documented in the repository's root `CLAUDE.md`. `--bare` must stay. What is the most effective fix?
options: Remove `--bare` and add `--allowedTools "Read"`, so the review loads `CLAUDE.md` again while only allowing Claude to read files during the run.
Prefix every rule in `CLAUDE.md` with "IMPORTANT", so the conventions carry more weight when Claude decides which findings to report.
Keep `--bare` and pass the review conventions and exclusions with `--append-system-prompt-file`, pointing at a conventions file in the repository.
Move the conventions into a project skill under `.claude/skills/review-conventions/`, so Claude loads them only when it performs reviews.
questions.why_correct: `--bare` saltea el auto-discovery, `CLAUDE.md` incluido: por eso desaparecieron las convenciones y subieron los falsos positivos. En bare mode el contexto se pasa con flags, y para sumar instrucciones existe `--append-system-prompt-file`. Cumplís la restricción y las convenciones vuelven a estar en cada review.

why_wrong.0: Recupera `CLAUDE.md`, pero sin `--bare` el `-p` vuelve a cargar los hooks y MCP servers del proyecto: rompe el requisito de seguridad.
why_wrong.1: `CLAUDE.md` no se está leyendo; ponerle IMPORTANT a algo que no se carga no cambia nada.
why_wrong.3: Bare mode también saltea el auto-discovery de skills: la convención seguiría sin cargarse.

questions.rule: `--bare` = sin `CLAUDE.md`. Convenciones persistentes en ese modo → `--append-system-prompt` o `--append-system-prompt-file`.
questions.source_quote: Add `--bare` to reduce startup time by skipping auto-discovery of your hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, installed plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md.

questions.scenario: A SaaS company uses the Code Review service on GitHub. Its monorepo has a root `CLAUDE.md` and a nested `services/api/CLAUDE.md` that says: "Queries built with the `sql` tagged template from `@acme/db` are parameterized and safe; do not flag them as SQL injection." PRs that change files under `services/api/` respect the rule. But PRs that only change `packages/db/src/reports.ts`, which uses the same tagged template, keep getting Important findings for SQL injection. Developers also run `/code-review` locally before pushing and want the same behavior there. Where should the team put this convention?
options: In the root `CLAUDE.md`, since a review reads it for every pull request and the local `/code-review` command follows `CLAUDE.md` files as well.
In a root `REVIEW.md`, since it holds review-only instructions that the service passes both to the agents that find issues and to those that verify them.
In a new `packages/db/CLAUDE.md` copied from the `services/api/` file, so each package that uses the tagged template has its own copy of the rule.
In `.claude/rules/sql.md` with `paths: ["**/*.ts"]`, so the rule loads whenever a TypeScript file in any package of the repo is touched.
questions.why_correct: El `CLAUDE.md` anidado solo se lee cuando el PR cambia archivos bajo esa ruta, y `packages/db/` no está debajo de `services/api/`. La convención vale para todo el repo, y el root `CLAUDE.md` lo leen tanto el servicio como el `/code-review` local.

why_wrong.1: Casi: el servicio lo leería, pero el `/code-review` local no lee `REVIEW.md`, y el equipo quiere el mismo comportamiento en los dos lados.
why_wrong.2: Funciona hoy para ese paquete, pero duplica la regla y se rompe en el próximo paquete que use el template: es una regla global.
why_wrong.3: La doc de Code Review no dice que el servicio lea `.claude/rules/`; lo que documenta son `CLAUDE.md` y `REVIEW.md`.

questions.rule: Convención que vale para todo el repo, en el servicio y en el review local → root `CLAUDE.md`.
questions.source_quote: A review reads the `CLAUDE.md` at your repository root and the `CLAUDE.md` files in the parent directories of each changed file.

questions.scenario: A logistics company built its own PR reviewer: a GitHub Actions step calls the Messages API with a system prompt loaded from `review/system.md` in the repo. The codebase intentionally uses a few patterns that look suspicious out of context, such as catching and logging `TimeoutError` without rethrowing inside retry wrappers, and `any` in generated DTO adapters. The prompt currently says "Be conservative and only report high-confidence findings." False positives on these patterns are still 40% of all comments, and last month a real null-dereference bug went unreported. What is the most effective change to `review/system.md`?
options: Replace the instruction with "Report only findings you are more than 90% sure about" and ask Claude to attach a confidence score to each finding.
Add few-shot examples that contrast each accepted pattern with a genuinely buggy variant, explaining why one is fine and the other is a real issue.
Add a list of every file that contains the accepted patterns and instruct Claude to skip any finding located in one of those files.
Add the sentence "These patterns are intentional" next to the conservative instruction, without changing anything else in the prompt.
questions.why_correct: 'Sé conservador' no sube la precisión, y encima bajó el recall (se escapó el null-deref). Ejemplos que contrastan el patrón aceptado con su variante con bug enseñan la frontera; como viven en `review/system.md`, se aplican en cada review, y el modelo generaliza a casos nuevos.

why_wrong.0: Es más de lo mismo: filtrar por confianza. La guía dice que instrucciones así no mejoran la precisión frente a criterios concretos.
why_wrong.2: Excluir archivos enteros esconde también los bugs reales que haya ahí (un retry wrapper puede tener un bug de verdad).
why_wrong.3: No dice qué patrones ni dónde está el límite: deja al modelo adivinando qué es 'intencional'.

questions.rule: Patrones aceptados que se marcan como bugs → few-shot 'aceptado vs. bug real' en el contexto persistente del review.
questions.source_quote: Providing few-shot examples distinguishing acceptable code patterns from genuine issues to reduce false positives while enabling generalization

questions.scenario: A team uses the Claude Code GitHub Action so developers can comment `@claude review this` on pull requests. Reviewers keep correcting the same false positives by replying in the PR thread: "We allow `console.error` in `scripts/`" and "Feature flags are read through `getFlag()`, never from `process.env` directly; that's intended." The next PR gets the same wrong comments again. The team also wants the Claude Code sessions on developers' laptops to follow the same conventions when they ask Claude to review their changes before pushing. What is the most effective fix?
options: Have reviewers start every `@claude` request with a short summary of the conventions, so each review run receives them as part of the prompt.
Add the conventions to `--append-system-prompt` through `claude_args` in the workflow file, so every Action run starts with them loaded.
Ask each developer to add the conventions to their own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so local sessions and review requests both follow them.
Write the conventions in the repository's root `CLAUDE.md`, which the Action reads on every run and local Claude Code sessions load at startup.
questions.why_correct: Las correcciones en el hilo del PR mueren con ese run. El root `CLAUDE.md` es el contexto persistente que la Action lee en cada ejecución y que las sesiones locales cargan al arrancar: una sola fuente, versionada con el repo, para los dos lugares.

why_wrong.0: Depende de que cada persona se acuerde y lo escriba bien: no es contexto persistente.
why_wrong.1: Casi: cubre cada run de la Action, pero las sesiones locales no ven el workflow. Terminás con las convenciones duplicadas en dos lugares.
why_wrong.2: El runner de la Action no tiene el `~/.claude/` de cada dev, y cada uno terminaría con su propia versión.

questions.rule: Convenciones de review para CI y local → root `CLAUDE.md`, versionado con el repo.
questions.source_quote: Create a `CLAUDE.md` file in your repository root to define code style guidelines, review criteria, project-specific rules, and preferred patterns. Claude follows these guidelines when creating PRs and responding to requests.

questions.scenario: A company on a Team plan uses the Code Review service on a repository whose default branch is protected. Reviews are accurate, but each PR gets 20 to 30 Nit comments about naming and small refactors, and developers have started ignoring whole reviews, Important findings included. The team keeps its review guidance in a project skill, `.claude/skills/review-style/SKILL.md`, which the root `REVIEW.md` includes with an `@` line. The lead added "Post at most five Nit comments per review" to that skill, but the nit volume didn't change at all. What should the team do?
options: Ask an Owner to lower the repository's review level, so each review is less thorough and naturally produces fewer Nit comments.
Move the nit guidance into the root `CLAUDE.md`, because Code Review reads `CLAUDE.md` as project context and applies it to every review.
Put the cap "Report at most five Nits per review" in the root `REVIEW.md` itself, or in a file beside it that `REVIEW.md` includes.
Keep the cap in the skill and add a frontmatter `description` saying the skill limits Nit comments, so the review knows to apply it.
questions.why_correct: La doc es explícita: Code Review no acepta el texto de una skill como motivo para excluir hallazgos ni para limitar nits. El tope va en el root `REVIEW.md` (o en un archivo al lado que `REVIEW.md` incluya), y con la rama default protegida se respeta.

why_wrong.0: Baja la cobertura de todo, Important incluidos, y no ataca lo que molesta, que son los nits.
why_wrong.1: `CLAUDE.md` es contexto de proyecto: la doc lo usa para reglas cuya violación se marca. El tope de nits es comportamiento del review, y la doc lo ubica en `REVIEW.md`.
why_wrong.3: La review solo recibe el body de `SKILL.md`, no el frontmatter; y aunque lo leyera, un tope de nits escrito en una skill no se acepta.

questions.rule: Exclusiones y topes de nits → root `REVIEW.md` (o un archivo incluido al lado), nunca dentro de una skill.
questions.source_quote: Write exclusions and Nit caps in `REVIEW.md` or a file beside it, not in an included skill.

questions.scenario: A 200-developer company uses the Code Review service with a protected default branch. Its root `REVIEW.md` had grown to 900 lines, so the platform team split it: the root file now holds a few lines plus `@docs/review/exclusions.md` and `@docs/review/security.md`, which keeps the review docs next to the rest of the engineering documentation. Since then, reviews again comment on lockfiles, on `src/gen/`, and on formatting issues that CI already enforces, all of which the exclusions file lists. The check run doesn't report any skipped include. Which change restores the exclusions?
options: Turn each `@` line into a Markdown link such as `[exclusions](docs/review/exclusions.md)`, so the review can follow the link to the rules.
Move `exclusions.md` and `security.md` to the repository root beside `REVIEW.md`, and include them with `@exclusions.md` and `@security.md`.
Convert the exclusions into a project skill at `.claude/skills/review-exclusions/SKILL.md` and include it from the root `REVIEW.md` by its `@` path.
Add a `REVIEW.md` inside `docs/review/` that includes the two files, since subdirectory `REVIEW.md` files apply on a protected default branch.
questions.why_correct: Las inclusiones con `@` solo toman archivos de la raíz, al lado de `REVIEW.md` (las skills son la excepción). Una ruta a un subdirectorio no se incluye y el `@` queda como texto plano, sin aviso en el check run. Con los archivos en la raíz, las exclusiones vuelven.

why_wrong.0: Un link de Markdown no es un include: la review ve el texto del link, no el contenido del archivo.
why_wrong.2: Casi: la skill se incluiría, pero Code Review no acepta el texto de una skill como motivo para excluir hallazgos. Las exclusiones seguirían sin aplicarse.
why_wrong.3: Un `REVIEW.md` de subdirectorio agrega checks para cambios *bajo ese directorio* (`docs/review/`), y un `@` dentro de él queda como texto plano.

questions.rule: Includes de `REVIEW.md`: archivos en la raíz, un solo nivel. Y las exclusiones nunca en una skill.
questions.source_quote: Location: move the file to the repository root. Except for a skill file, a path into a subdirectory such as `@docs/review-rules.md` isn't included.

questions.scenario: An insurance company's CI runs `claude -p "Review the staged diff against our conventions and report violations" --setting-sources user` on a Linux runner. The security team chose `--setting-sources user` so that a `.claude/settings.json` committed on a PR branch can never change permissions or add hooks in CI. The team's review conventions (accepted patterns such as returning `Either` from service methods, and exclusions such as `migrations/` and `*.snap` files) live in `.claude/rules/review.md`. Reviews now flag those accepted patterns and snapshot files on almost every PR. The security setting must not change. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add `project` back to `--setting-sources`, so the review loads the project's rules again and the conventions apply on every run.
Pass the conventions with `--append-system-prompt-file` pointing at a conventions file, so they apply on every run without loading project settings.
Add `paths: ["**/*"]` to the rule's frontmatter, so it becomes a path-scoped rule that loads on demand when Claude reads matching files.
Rename the rule to `00-review.md` so it sorts first in `.claude/rules/` and gets loaded before any other project rule in the run.
questions.why_correct: Sin `project` en `--setting-sources`, las reglas de `.claude/rules/` no se cargan: por eso desaparecieron las convenciones. `--append-system-prompt-file` mete el texto en cada run sin tocar la restricción de seguridad.

why_wrong.0: Arregla las convenciones, pero vuelve a cargar los settings del proyecto (permisos, hooks): rompe el requisito de seguridad.
why_wrong.2: Casi: antes de v2.1.211 las reglas que cargan on demand (como las de `paths`) se cargaban igual; desde esa versión también se saltean si excluís `project`.
why_wrong.3: El problema no es el orden: con esa configuración no se carga ninguna regla de proyecto.

questions.rule: Excluir `project` de `--setting-sources` apaga `.claude/rules/`. Convenciones en CI → un flag explícito.
questions.source_quote: Project rules are skipped if you exclude `project` from `--setting-sources`.

questions.scenario: A platform team runs a review service over the Messages API for 60 repositories. For each PR the service opens a "review session": the first request sends a 6k-token system prompt with that repo's accepted patterns and exclusions, plus the first changed file. To save tokens, the follow-up requests for the remaining files send only the new file's diff and the instruction "Review this file with the same conventions as before." Precision is good on the first file of each PR but drops sharply on later files, which get flagged for the very patterns the conventions allow. Cost matters at this volume. What is the most effective fix?
options: Send the repo's conventions in the system prompt of every request, and mark that prefix for prompt caching to keep the repeated tokens cheap.
Return a session ID from the first request and include it in each follow-up, so the API links them to the conventions sent earlier.
Review all of a PR's changed files in one request with the conventions at the top, so the model only needs to see the conventions once.
Shorten the conventions to a one-paragraph summary and send it with each follow-up, keeping the full version only for the first file.
questions.why_correct: La Messages API no guarda estado: cada request se procesa solo con lo que manda, así que los archivos 2 a N no ven las convenciones. Mandarlas en cada request (contexto persistente aplicado en cada review) y cachear ese prefijo con prompt caching mantiene el costo bajo.

why_wrong.1: No existe memoria server-side en la Messages API que vincule requests por un ID: cualquier opción así es falsa.
why_wrong.2: Resuelve el estado, pero arma un request gigante por PR: más riesgo de truncamiento y de dilución de la atención en PRs grandes.
why_wrong.3: Recortar las convenciones es perder justo los patrones aceptados que evitan los falsos positivos; y el costo ya lo resuelve prompt caching.

questions.rule: API stateless: el contexto persistente viaja en cada request (y se cachea).
questions.source_quote: The Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API.

questions.scenario: A 40-developer team uses Claude Code with a root `CLAUDE.md` that says "Handle errors by throwing typed exceptions; never return error codes." Two years later, the payments team adopted a result-type pattern and added `.claude/rules/payments.md`, scoped with `paths: ["services/payments/**"]`, saying "Return `Result<T, E>`; do not throw from service methods." When developers ask Claude to review payments code, it flags the `Result` returns as violations in roughly half the runs and accepts them in the other half, on the very same file. Both instructions are loaded in those sessions. What should the team do first?
options: Prefix the payments rule with "IMPORTANT: this overrides CLAUDE.md", so Claude gives it priority whenever both instructions are in context.
Move the payments rule into `services/payments/CLAUDE.md`, since nested `CLAUDE.md` files always take precedence over path-scoped rules.
Resolve the contradiction: scope the root rule so it excludes `services/payments/`, or reword both so the two instructions no longer conflict.
Raise the effort level for review requests, so Claude reasons longer about which of the two error-handling instructions applies to a file.
questions.why_correct: El síntoma (mitad y mitad sobre el mismo archivo) es el que describe la doc: con dos instrucciones contradictorias, Claude puede elegir una arbitrariamente. El primer paso es eliminar la contradicción para que haya una sola convención por zona del código.

why_wrong.0: Puede inclinar la balanza, pero deja la contradicción en el contexto: sigue siendo guidance peleando contra otra guidance.
why_wrong.1: La doc no establece esa precedencia; seguís teniendo dos reglas contradictorias cargadas a la vez.
why_wrong.3: Más razonamiento no elimina el conflicto: sigue sin haber una única regla correcta para elegir.

questions.rule: Instrucciones contradictorias → resultados al azar. Primero resolvé el conflicto.
questions.source_quote: Consistency: if two instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily.

questions.scenario: Developers at a retail company run `/code-review` in Claude Code on their Windows laptops before pushing. Two complaints dominate: reviews keep flagging the team's accepted use of `Promise.allSettled` without inspecting rejected results in fire-and-forget analytics calls, and some findings are speculative ("this might be slow"). The team's root `REVIEW.md` lists that pattern as accepted, and it works fine for the Code Review service on GitHub. Developers want local reviews to apply the same accepted pattern and to show only the findings Claude is most confident in. Which combination achieves both?
options: Add the accepted pattern to the root `REVIEW.md` under "Do not report", and run `/code-review max` so the review verifies each finding more thoroughly.
Document the accepted pattern in the root `CLAUDE.md`, and run `/code-review --max-findings 3` so only the top three findings are reported.
Run `/code-review REVIEW.md` so the review loads the accepted patterns from that file, and run it at `low` effort for fewer false positives.
Document the accepted pattern in the root `CLAUDE.md`, and run `/code-review low` so the review reports only the findings it's most confident in.
questions.why_correct: El `/code-review` local lee `CLAUDE.md` y no `REVIEW.md`: el patrón aceptado tiene que estar en `CLAUDE.md` para valer en los dos lados. Y la doc dice que en `low` el review reporta los hallazgos de mayor confianza: menos falsos positivos.

why_wrong.0: El comando local no lee `REVIEW.md`, y `max` amplía la cobertura: más hallazgos, no menos especulativos.
why_wrong.1: Casi: `CLAUDE.md` es lo correcto, pero `--max-findings` limita la cantidad; no garantiza que los que queden sean los más confiables.
why_wrong.2: El texto después del comando es el *target* del review: revisaría el archivo `REVIEW.md`, no lo usaría como instrucciones.

questions.rule: `/code-review` local: reglas en `CLAUDE.md`; menos falsos positivos con effort `low`.
questions.source_quote: At `low`, the review reports the findings it's most confident in, so you see fewer false positives.
